Definitions first, then the three questions that have hard answers in the tree, then the two you asked me to start. One of the facts below changes the picture on both the type checking and the speed.

## The words

- **Reshape**: take the elements of an array in order and lay them out in a different shape. `(2,3)⍴` of six numbers is a two-by-three matrix. Hsu's layout lives on this: the parameters are one flat vector of 4192 numbers and each weight matrix is a reshape of a slice of it.
- **Ravel** (`,`): the opposite, flatten any array into a vector in row-major order. `⊃,/,¨` in the program ravels nine gradient matrices and joins them into the one flat gradient vector.
- **Planes**: a rank-3 array is a stack of matrices; each matrix in the stack is a plane. The attention block is one plane per (document, head) pair, and `⍤2` means "do this to every plane".
- **Gather**: pick rows of a matrix by a list of indices. `wte[ids;]` takes the embedding row of every token in the batch.
- **Outer product** (`∘.f`): apply `f` to every pair from two vectors, giving a matrix. `ids∘.=⍳27` compares each token id with each of the 27 vocabulary indices, which is the one-hot matrix; `(⍳16)∘.≥⍳16` compares positions and is the causal mask.

## Ring, Field, and which specification

I search the in-repo `Specification/` tree, which is the later draft with the implementers' notes, not the frozen 1.0. On the algebraic library the draft's chapter is `advanced-lib/algebraic-constraints.tex`, and its `Ring` and `Field` declarations are there as commented-out LaTeX, lines 1541 and 1761, never made normative. The shipped library has `AdditiveGroup`, `MultiplicativeRing` and an `AnyMultiplicativeRing` marker, nothing more; and, as the Fable review found, the shipped `RR64` does not even satisfy the spec's `AdditiveGroup` bound. On positional arguments, the same draft: nothing, in any chapter or in the parser.

## The `nat` parameters, and the fact that changes things

You have the intent exactly right, and there are two reasons your expectation is not met here, one of them new.

The first I gave: the specification says `nat` parameters are "instantiated at runtime", so they were never meant as compile-time constants that a code generator folds; the design is dimension checking, not dimension-driven optimization. I know of no paper on this specifically; the published type-system work from the team (the OOPSLA 2011 paper on modular multiple dispatch, in `research/README.md`) is about overloading, not sizes.

The second is in `repo-internals.md` and I should have led with it: the static type checker exists, in Scala, and the walk interpreter never runs it. The `walk` command turns it off, and the phase is a no-op, so the interpreter runs untyped and every "type error" we have ever seen from it is a run-time dispatch failure. The `compile` command turns the checker on. So the compile-time error you are asking about, a mismatched dimension refused before running, is exactly what the compiled path is for, and it is the path this project has characterized but not finished.

That also answers the class-loader question. The bytecode compiler lowers every type to a JVM reference type and emits a dispatch method per overloaded name; there is no place in it where size checks would be generated, because in the design they are the checker's job, ahead of code generation, and the checker is the part that runs only on that path.

## The fast path, and the walking skeleton

The narrow path you describe exists and has numbers. `compiled-path-gaps.md` measured the bytecode compiler against the interpreter on the constructs microGPT is made of: 6.8× on a scalar loop, 8.9× on object allocation and operator calls, numerics identical to the last digit. The written record agrees with your reading, and it says where the performance mandate went.

**The money left in 2006.** Fortress was Sun's entry in DARPA's High Productivity Computing Systems program. When DARPA chose the Phase III vendors in late 2006 it kept Cray and IBM and dropped Sun. From then on Fortress was a Sun Labs research project on a research budget, and the work that followed was the specification, the type system, and the interpreter. The compiler to JVM bytecode only started around 2008.

**What they said stopped them.** Steele's July 2012 wrap-up post, which we hold as an extract at `research/extracts/fortress-websites-wayback.md`, does not blame arithmetic speed. It says they hit "severe technical challenges having to do with the mismatch between the (rather ambitious) Fortress type system and a virtual machine not designed to support it (that would be every currently available VM, not just JVM)." The runtime class generation for generics was their attempt at that mismatch, and it is written up in the papers under `Papers/RuntimeInstantiation` in the original tree. So the boxing and the unspecialized generics were not an oversight they planned to fix later. They were the frontier they were still fighting when the project ended.

**Was there a plan for an optimizing compiler?** Not as a document I can point to. The bet, stated in the early design papers, was that a JVM target would inherit HotSpot's optimization for free and that the language's implicit parallelism would deliver the speed at scale. Both halves depend on the semantic overhead being compiled away, and they never got to that stage. The code generator does contain some unboxing and specialization code, which I have only seen by name and not read.

Your verdict stands on the evidence: expressivity and the parallel model were the research, and performance was deferred to a runtime that could not carry it.

If you want the recorded plans collected properly, a scout through `Papers/`, the spec's implementation notes, and the 2008 to 2012 commit messages is one Opus worker. Not launching it unasked.

This repository preserves that codebase: the complete surviving history,
January 2007 through August 2012, carried forward so that it still builds
and runs on today's Java platform.

## History

**2003–2006: DARPA HPCS.** Fortress began in 2003 as Sun's language effort
within DARPA's High Productivity Computing Systems program, run by Sun
Labs' Programming Language Research Group. When DARPA narrowed HPCS funding
in late 2006, Sun continued Fortress as a research project.

**2007–2008: open source and Fortress 1.0.** The code — at that point the
reference interpreter — was opened in January 2007 (this repository's
history begins on 4 January 2007). The 1.0 specification, with a matching
interpreter release, followed in March 2008.

**2008–2012: the type-system frontier.** Work shifted from the interpreter
to compiling Fortress to the JVM, and to the hard theory: the Meet Rule,
the return type rule, and run-time instantiation of generics. Steele,
looking back in 2016, was frank about where that frontier stalled:
*"'Non-trivial' is a euphemism for 'exponential cost' […] So we had a grand
vision, but could not quite pull it off."* The original repository closes
in August 2012 with that problem still open — its last commits record the
attempt.

**2012: wind-down.** Oracle Labs
[concluded the project in the summer of 2012](https://web.archive.org/web/20121007034544/https://blogs.oracle.com/projectfortress/entry/fortress_wrapping_up).

**2015–2016: coda.** Steele revisited Fortress in a pair of retrospective
talks: [*Four Solutions to a Trivial Problem*](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ftcIcn8AmSY)
at Google (December 2015), on the generator/reducer decomposition at the
language's core, and the JuliaCon 2016 keynote
[*Fortress Features and Lessons Learned*](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EZD3Scuv02g),
the fullest account of what the project proved and where it got stuck.

**Ring, Field, and the `RR64` finding.** These are names for what a set of values can do. An additive group: you can add, subtract, and there is a zero. A ring: an additive group where you can also multiply, with a one. A field: a ring where you can also divide by anything but zero. Integers form a ring, reals form a field, matrices of a given size form a ring but not a field. The point of the traits is that once a type declares which of these it is, everything written in terms of the operations comes for free. The finding: the specification's array chapter writes its element bound as `T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]`, and the shipped `RR64` is not declared to satisfy it, so a function written the spec's way refuses real numbers (probe `v04b_groupbound.out.0`); the bound that works is `T extends Number`, which is not algebra but a name. """tlib: the curator's messages, and the coordinating session's message that each one answered,
read along the transcript's reply chain (standard library).

His messages are exactly what explorations/coordinator/curator-profile/show.py's load() gives: the
live transcripts, the backup copies in /home/user/fortress-transcripts-blinded (the .parts folders
and the copy until 2026-10-08T15-41 included) and the first session on the `transcripts` branch;
deduplicated by uuid; queued messages with the time he sent them. load_msgs() rebuilds that list
from a per-file index (cache below) with show.py's own functions, in show.py's file order, so the
list is the same; tests.py checks it against show.load().

The message he answered (Talk.answered) follows the chain of the transcript itself: each line's
parentUuid (a compaction's logicalParentUuid), back from his message. Every line on the chain is
one of:
  his     a message of his (show.py's test), or his message queued while a turn ran, delivered
          into that turn (a queued_command attachment that is not a notification)
  text    an assistant line of the session (not a sidechain) holding text
  note    a prompt that is not his: Stop-hook feedback, an agent's message or hand-back, a task
          notification (also a scheduled check-in), a system reminder, a prompt starting '<'
  pass    everything else, passed through: tool calls and results, attachments, hook summaries,
          and the prompts that only continue a turn (a compaction summary, "Continue from where
          you left off", a worker restart notice, a skill's text, an image, a local command)
Going back from his message, the texts met are collected; reaching a note drops them as a turn
not to him (they are listed as skipped), and reaching a prompt of his makes them the answer: the
coordinator's whole turn after that prompt, every text of it, oldest first. A text written after
he sent his message (a queued message is delivered late) is listed apart, not taken. The turns to
him further back on the chain are kept too (Talk.answered(..., earlier=3)), for a reply to an
older question. Two checks on the rule: a skipped turn that answers a notification and ends with
an ask to him (ASK: a question mark, "The ask", "I recommend", "your yes", ...) is marked 'asks',
since the coordinator often relays an agent's result with a question; and when his message
quotes lines ("> ..."), the newest text on the chain that holds them is found ('quoted').
Talk.reply(m) gives the coordinator's turn after his message m.

Cache: ./cache/tx3-<path hash>.pickle, one per transcript file, holding the file's index and its
key (path, size and mtime; the blob id for the `transcripts` branch). A file whose key changed is
indexed again and its entry replaced. INDEX_VERSION is part of the key.
"""

The measurement worker is running. It is checking each of the 13 errors for a fix that needs no new language, and whether the code generator can compile the `NatParam` clause.

**Did the team's compiler have any work on compiled arrays?** Almost none. Its own small library has two array-like types, `ZZ32Vector` and `StringVector`. They are hand-written Java classes, every element is boxed, and no test of the team's builds or indexes one at run time. It has no general array type.

**Do we have to reinvent arrays?** No. The team wrote a full array family in Fortress, in the interpreter's library: `Array1` to `Array3`, `Vector`, `Matrix`, their factories, and sizes as type parameters. The plan is for the compiler to compile that library. What's ours to add:
- The checker had to learn sizes. The team's checker stopped with "Not yet implemented" on every size parameter. We built that part.
- Sizes had to exist while the program runs. We built that part too.
- The native store under the arrays needs a compiled version. That comes with the switch-over.
- Arrays of unboxed doubles come after that.

**How `NatParam` got onto our path.** It's the team's own array code. Here's their factory for an array whose size is computed at run time:
```
array[\E\](x: ZZ32): Array[\E,ZZ32\] =
  __arr1(__thrower[\E\], reflect(x))

__arr1[\E, nat n\](w: () -> E, x: N[\n\])
    : Array1[\E,0,n\] = array1[\E,n\]()
```
`reflect(x)` turns the number into a `NatParam`. `__arr1` needs an `N[\n\]`, so that it has a size `n` to build the array with. The link between the two is one line the team wrote in 2007 and left as a comment:
```
trait NatParam
  comprises { N[\n\] } where [\ nat n \]
```
Their own note above it explains it: every `NatParam` is an `N[\n\]`, so you can pass one to a function that takes `N[\n\]`, and inside that function `n` becomes a size. Walk always ran this code, because walk looks at the actual value. The compiled checker can't look at values, so it refused 10 lines of the team's array code. Batch 13 uncommented the line and taught the checker that one rule.

So this isn't the general `where` feature. It's one narrow form, a variable inside a `comprises` clause, with the team's design written next to it.

**Can the other fix apply to `NatParam`?** I don't think it can. The other fixes were to drop the code or rewrite it with tools the paths already run.
- **Dropping it:** every array whose size is computed at run time goes through these lines.
- **A `typecase`:** it lists a fixed set of cases, and sizes have no limit. The clause is what says "some size".
- **An array that keeps its length in a field instead of its type:** possible in principle, and it's one of your open array questions. But the team didn't write one. It would also give up checked sizes for every array built from a run-time number, and microGPT has such arrays where its sizes come from the data.

That's why batch 13 took the clause: the team left a written design for it. Building it went by the rule I proposed: follow what the team left, and add nothing they didn't.
